idiom_name: private volatile T cell; double-checked accessor
implementation_notes: The JMM-corrected classic: the volatile field carries the happens-before edge introduced by JSR-133, so a reader that sees a non-null reference is guaranteed to see the constructed object, and the fast path is one volatile read taken into a local variable. Before Java 5 this exact code was broken, which is why the pattern has its reputation; the JDK has no Lazy<T>, so this remains the realization for per-instance cells that a holder class cannot serve.
pitfalls: Dropping volatile (or publishing through a non-volatile alias) reintroduces the JMM failure: a reader can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object.
Reading the field twice instead of into a local variable can return null on the second read and defeats the fast path; the local copy is the documented idiom.
Synchronising on this, on a Class object, or on a pooled String invites deadlock with external code; use a private final lock object.
Serialization and reflection can create a second instance behind the accessor's back - the pattern guards construction, not instance identity.

variants.name: initialization-on-demand holder class
variants.idiom_name: private static class Holder { static final T INSTANCE = build(); }
variants.implementation_notes: The idiomatic Java answer: the value lives in a nested class that is only initialised when its field is first referenced, and the JVM's class-initialisation procedure (JLS 12.4.2's initialization lock LC) gives exactly-once execution plus safe publication with no check at all in the accessor. It replaces volatile-plus-double-check for static state and is what the JSR-133 FAQ points to; keep the volatile form for per-instance cells where reaching the holder would be triggered by any other member access.
pitfalls: Class initialisation is one-shot: if the initialiser fails, the class is marked erroneous and every later access throws ExceptionInInitializerError or NoClassDefFoundError - there is no retry and no reset.
It cannot serve per-instance laziness (each instance would need its own holder) and any access to the holder's members triggers the build.
Circular class initialisation between two threads deadlocks, so initialisers must not call back into unrelated lazy holders.
Reflection, DI containers or serialisation that touch the holder early can initialise the value during start-up, silently defeating the laziness.
